claim: STEAP1 was first discovered owing to its high level of expression in prostate cancer cells.
source: Six-transmembrane epithelial antigen of the prostate 1 (STEAP1) was first discovered owing to its high level of expression in prostate cancer cells (Hubert et al., 1999).
evidence: Supported by citation to Hubert et al., 1999

claim: STEAP2–4 have metal ion reductase activities.
source: Discovery of STEAP2–4 soon followed, and further analyses show that STEAP2–4 have metal ion reductase activities (Grunewald et al., 2012; Ohgami et al., 2006).
evidence: Supported by citations to Grunewald et al., 2012 and Ohgami et al., 2006

claim: STEAP3 was identified as a ferrireductase required for iron uptake in erythroid cells.
source: STEAP3 was identified as a ferrireductase required for iron uptake in erythroid cells (Ohgami et al., 2006; Ohgami et al., 2005).
evidence: Supported by citations to Ohgami et al., 2006 and Ohgami et al., 2005

claim: STEAP2–4 are found overexpressed in many types of cancer cells.
source: STEAP2–4 are also found overexpressed in many types of cancer cells, suggesting their involvement in cancer initiation or progression (Hubert et al., 1999; Gomes et al., 2013; Rocha et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citations to Hubert et al., 1999; Gomes et al., 2013; Rocha et al., 2021

claim: Each STEAP protein has a transmembrane domain (TMD) which consists of six transmembrane helices.
source: Each STEAP protein has a transmembrane domain (TMD) which consists of six transmembrane helices (TM), and STEAP2–4, but not STEAP1, also have an N-terminal intracellular oxidoreductase domain (OxRD) (Pick, 2023; Kleven et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to Pick, 2023 and Kleven et al., 2015

claim: STEAP2–4, but not STEAP1, have an N-terminal intracellular oxidoreductase domain (OxRD).
source: Each STEAP protein has a transmembrane domain (TMD) which consists of six transmembrane helices (TM), and STEAP2–4, but not STEAP1, also have an N-terminal intracellular oxidoreductase domain (OxRD) (Pick, 2023; Kleven et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to Pick, 2023 and Kleven et al., 2015

claim: TMD of the STEAP family of proteins are homologous to membrane-embedded reductases including mammalian NADPH oxidases (NOX) and dual oxidases (DUOX), and bacterial and yeast ferric reductases.
source: TMD of the STEAP family of proteins are homologous to membrane-embedded reductases including mammalian NADPH oxidases (NOX) and dual oxidases (DUOX), and bacterial and yeast ferric reductases (Zhang et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to Zhang et al., 2013

claim: The structures of NOX and DUOX show that their TMD binds two heme prosthetic groups, each ligated to a pair of conserved histidine residues from TMs 3 and 5.
source: The structures of NOX and DUOX show that their TMD binds two heme prosthetic groups, each ligated to a pair of conserved histidine residues from TMs 3 and 5; one heme is close to the intracellular side and the other close to the extracellular side of the TMD (Wu et al., 2021; Sun, 2020; Liu et al., 2022; Magnani et al., 2017; Oosterheert et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citations to Wu et al., 2021; Sun, 2020; Liu et al., 2022; Magnani et al., 2017; Oosterheert et al., 2020

claim: In NOX and DUOX, one heme is close to the intracellular side and the other close to the extracellular side of the TMD.
source: The structures of NOX and DUOX show that their TMD binds two heme prosthetic groups, each ligated to a pair of conserved histidine residues from TMs 3 and 5; one heme is close to the intracellular side and the other close to the extracellular side of the TMD (Wu et al., 2021; Sun, 2020; Liu et al., 2022; Magnani et al., 2017; Oosterheert et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citations to Wu et al., 2021; Sun, 2020; Liu et al., 2022; Magnani et al., 2017; Oosterheert et al., 2020

claim: In NOX or DUOX, the OxRD binds both NADPH and FAD.
source: In NOX or DUOX, the OxRD binds both NADPH and FAD, and the cross-membrane electron transfer chain starts with hydride transfer from NADPH to FAD, and then sequentially to the intracellular and extracellular hemes, and finally to the substrate.
evidence: Stated as established knowledge about NOX/DUOX electron transfer mechanism

claim: In NOX or DUOX, the cross-membrane electron transfer chain starts with hydride transfer from NADPH to FAD, and then sequentially to the intracellular and extracellular hemes, and finally to the substrate.
source: In NOX or DUOX, the OxRD binds both NADPH and FAD, and the cross-membrane electron transfer chain starts with hydride transfer from NADPH to FAD, and then sequentially to the intracellular and extracellular hemes, and finally to the substrate.
evidence: Stated as established knowledge about NOX/DUOX electron transfer mechanism

claim: The structure of STEAP4 shows that only one heme is present in the TMD and it corresponds to the extracellular heme in NOX or DUOX.
source: The structure of STEAP4, on the other hand, shows that only one heme is present in the TMD and it corresponds to the extracellular heme in NOX or DUOX (Oosterheert et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to Oosterheert et al., 2018

claim: In STEAP4, the FAD straddles OxRD and TMD with the isoalloxazine ring of FAD binding at the equivalent position of the intracellular heme in NOX and DUOX and the nucleotide moiety of FAD binding to the OxRD.
source: In STEAP4, the FAD straddles OxRD and TMD with the isoalloxazine ring of FAD binding at the equivalent position of the intracellular heme in NOX and DUOX and the nucleotide moiety of FAD binding to the OxRD (Figure 1).
evidence: Supported by reference to Figure 1 showing structural comparison

claim: The isoalloxazine ring of FAD is too far away from the nicotinamide ring of NADPH to receive hydride in STEAP4.
source: While this configuration allows electron transfer between FAD and heme, the isoalloxazine ring is too far away from the nicotinamide ring of NADPH to receive hydride.
evidence: Based on structural analysis of STEAP4

claim: The isoalloxazine ring of FAD must dissociate from the TMD and move closer to the nicotinamide ring of NADPH for hydride transfer in STEAPs.
source: Thus, the isoalloxazine ring of FAD must dissociate from the TMD and move closer to the nicotinamide ring of NADPH for hydride transfer.
evidence: Logical inference from the distance constraint

claim: FAD does not stay tightly bound to the STEAP protein and can become diffusible after its reduction.
source: Although the isoalloxazine ring of FAD must assume different conformations during the redox cycles in STEAPs, its adenosine moiety could stay bound to the OxRD. However, here we show evidence that FAD does not stay tightly bound to the STEAP protein and can become diffusible after its reduction.
evidence: Supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript

claim: Reduced FAD readily reduces STEAP1.
source: We found that reduced FAD (as FADH-) readily reduces STEAP1, shown by the fast decrease in the Soret absorbance of ferric heme (A413) and the concomitant increase in the Soret absorbance of ferrous heme (A427) (Figure 2A).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A

claim: The time course of A427 increase in STEAP1 reduction by FADH- is biphasic.
source: The time course of A427 increase is biphasic.
evidence: Supported by kinetic analysis of experimental data

claim: The fast phase of STEAP1 reduction by FADH- has a rate constant of 7.7 s–1 and accounts for 60% of the total change at A427.
source: The fast phase has a rate constant of 7.7 s–1 and accounts for 60% of the total change at A427, and the slow phase, 0.67 s–1 and 40% (Figure 2B).
evidence: Supported by kinetic data shown in Figure 2B

claim: The slow phase of STEAP1 reduction by FADH- has a rate constant of 0.67 s–1 and accounts for 40% of the total change.
source: The fast phase has a rate constant of 7.7 s–1 and accounts for 60% of the total change at A427, and the slow phase, 0.67 s–1 and 40% (Figure 2B).
evidence: Supported by kinetic data shown in Figure 2B

claim: The rate constants of both phases of STEAP1 reduction exhibit dependence on [FADH-].
source: The rate constants of both phases exhibit dependence on [FADH-].
evidence: Supported by kinetic analysis

claim: For the fast phase of STEAP1 reduction by FADH-, the Vmax is estimated at 12 s–1 and KM at 4.7 μM.
source: The Vmax and KM are estimated 12 s–1 and 4.7 μM for the fast phase, and the parameters are estimated 0.9 s–1 and 2.7 μM for the slow phase (Figure 2B, inset).
evidence: Supported by kinetic parameter estimation shown in Figure 2B inset

claim: For the slow phase of STEAP1 reduction by FADH-, the Vmax is estimated at 0.9 s–1 and KM at 2.7 μM.
source: The Vmax and KM are estimated 12 s–1 and 4.7 μM for the fast phase, and the parameters are estimated 0.9 s–1 and 2.7 μM for the slow phase (Figure 2B, inset).
evidence: Supported by kinetic parameter estimation shown in Figure 2B inset

claim: In STEAP4 structure, a phenylalanine side chain (Phe359) is positioned between the isoalloxazine ring of FAD and the heme.
source: In STEAP4 structure, a phenylalanine side chain (Phe359) is positioned between the isoalloxazine ring of FAD and the heme and is thought to mediate electron transfer from FAD to heme (Oosterheert et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to Oosterheert et al., 2018

claim: Phe359 in STEAP4 is thought to mediate electron transfer from FAD to heme.
source: In STEAP4 structure, a phenylalanine side chain (Phe359) is positioned between the isoalloxazine ring of FAD and the heme and is thought to mediate electron transfer from FAD to heme (Oosterheert et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to Oosterheert et al., 2018

claim: In STEAP1–3, the equivalent residue to Phe359 in STEAP4 is a leucine, Leu230 in STEAP1.
source: In STEAP1–3, the equivalent residue is a leucine, Leu230 in STEAP1 (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Supported by structural comparison shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A

claim: The UV-Vis spectrum of L230G STEAP1 is identical to that of the wild-type (WT) STEAP1.
source: The UV-Vis spectrum of L230G STEAP1 is identical to that of the wild-type (WT) STEAP1 (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B), indicating that the mutation does not perturb heme binding.
evidence: Supported by spectroscopic data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1B

claim: The L230G mutation does not perturb heme binding in STEAP1.
source: The UV-Vis spectrum of L230G STEAP1 is identical to that of the wild-type (WT) STEAP1 (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B), indicating that the mutation does not perturb heme binding.
evidence: Inferred from identical UV-Vis spectra

claim: The heme in L230G STEAP1 is reduced by FADH- more than five times slower than in WT STEAP1.
source: These results indicate that the heme in L230G STEAP1 is reduced by FADH- more than five times slower than in WT STEAP1, suggesting that the side chain of Leu230 is involved in mediating electron transfer between FAD and heme in STEAPs.
evidence: Supported by comparison of kinetic data

claim: The side chain of Leu230 is involved in mediating electron transfer between FAD and heme in STEAPs.
source: These results indicate that the heme in L230G STEAP1 is reduced by FADH- more than five times slower than in WT STEAP1, suggesting that the side chain of Leu230 is involved in mediating electron transfer between FAD and heme in STEAPs.
evidence: Inferred from the slower reduction rate in L230G mutant

claim: Cytochrome b5 reductase (b5R) catalyzes the reduction of a tightly bound FAD by NADH.
source: b5R catalyzes the reduction of a tightly bound FAD by NADH and is known to reduce the heme on cytochrome b5 (Hall et al., 2022; Shen et al., 2022).
evidence: Supported by citations to Hall et al., 2022 and Shen et al., 2022

claim: b5R is known to reduce the heme on cytochrome b5.
source: b5R catalyzes the reduction of a tightly bound FAD by NADH and is known to reduce the heme on cytochrome b5 (Hall et al., 2022; Shen et al., 2022).
evidence: Supported by citations to Hall et al., 2022 and Shen et al., 2022

claim: Under anaerobic conditions, STEAP1 does not react with NADH.
source: Under anaerobic conditions, STEAP1 does not react with NADH but in the presence of both b5R and NADH, the A427 absorbance increases indicating reduction of the heme on STEAP1 (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A

claim: In the presence of both b5R and NADH, the A427 absorbance increases indicating reduction of the heme on STEAP1.
source: Under anaerobic conditions, STEAP1 does not react with NADH but in the presence of both b5R and NADH, the A427 absorbance increases indicating reduction of the heme on STEAP1 (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A

claim: Three spectral species, A, B, and C, are resolved in the reaction of STEAP1 with b5R and NADH with rate constants of 177.9 s–1 (A to B) and 0.13 s–1 (B to C).
source: Three spectral species, A, B, and C, are resolved with rate constants of 177.9 (±35.3) s–1 (A to B) and 0.13 (±0.006) s–1 (B to C), respectively (Figure 3A, inset).
evidence: Supported by spectral deconvolution shown in Figure 3A inset

claim: Spectral species A corresponds to ferric STEAP1 plus oxidized b5R.
source: Spectral species A corresponds to ferric STEAP1 plus oxidized b5R while species C is ferrous STEAP1 with fully reduced b5R.
evidence: Interpretation of spectral data

claim: Spectral species C is ferrous STEAP1 with fully reduced b5R.
source: Spectral species A corresponds to ferric STEAP1 plus oxidized b5R while species C is ferrous STEAP1 with fully reduced b5R.
evidence: Interpretation of spectral data

claim: Spectral intermediate species B contains partially reduced b5R and a ferric heme.
source: A spectral intermediate species B can be identified with decreased absorbance in 420–500 nm range but little or no change in the Soret range when compared to A (Figure 3A, inset), indicating that the intermediate B contains partially reduced b5R and a ferric heme.
evidence: Inferred from spectral characteristics shown in Figure 3A inset

claim: The B to C conversion reflects electron transfer from reduced b5R to STEAP1.
source: The B to C conversion reflects electron transfer from reduced b5R to STEAP1 (Figure 3A), indicating that STEAP1 can form an electron transfer chain with b5R.
evidence: Interpretation of kinetic data

claim: STEAP1 can form an electron transfer chain with b5R.
source: The B to C conversion reflects electron transfer from reduced b5R to STEAP1 (Figure 3A), indicating that STEAP1 can form an electron transfer chain with b5R.
evidence: Inferred from electron transfer kinetics

claim: b5R binds STEAP1 with a KD of ~5.9 µM.
source: Using bio-layer interferometry (BLI) assay, we measured the affinity between b5R and STEAP1 and found that b5R binds STEAP1 with a KD of ~5.9 µM (Figure 3—figure supplement 2).

claim: b5R can dock onto STEAP1 to establish an electron transfer chain.
source: Nonetheless, our BLI data demonstrates that b5R can dock onto STEAP1 to establish an electron transfer chain.
evidence: Inferred from BLI binding data

claim: The rate constant from B to C is significantly slower in L230G STEAP1 than in WT STEAP1.

evidence: Supported by comparison of kinetic data shown in Figure 3B inset

claim: Leu230 is involved in the electron transfer from b5R to STEAP1.
source: On the other hand, the rate constant from B to C, which is electron transfer rate from reduced b5R to the heme, is significantly slower in L230G STEAP1 than in WT STEAP1 (Figure 3B, inset), suggesting that Leu230 is involved in the electron transfer from b5R to STEAP1.
evidence: Inferred from slower electron transfer in L230G mutant

claim: Purified STEAP2 elutes as a single peak in size exclusion chromatography.

evidence: Supported by chromatography data shown in Figure 4A

claim: The elution volume of STEAP2 is consistent with STEAP2 being a homotrimer.
source: We expressed and purified human STEAP2, which elutes as a single peak in size exclusion chromatography and the elution volume is consistent with STEAP2 being a homotrimer (Figure 4A).

claim: A prominent heme absorption peak is present in the purified STEAP2.
source: A prominent heme absorption peak is present in the purified STEAP2, and the heme content typically ranges from 70% to 90%.

claim: The heme content in purified STEAP2 typically ranges from 70% to 90%.
source: A prominent heme absorption peak is present in the purified STEAP2, and the heme content typically ranges from 70% to 90%.

claim: FAD is detected in the purified STEAP2 at a level typically lower than 20%.

claim: No NADP(H) is detected in the purified STEAP2.
source: No NADP(H) is detected in the purified STEAP2, suggesting that its association with STEAP2 is more transient than either heme or FAD.

claim: The association of NADP(H) with STEAP2 is more transient than either heme or FAD.
source: No NADP(H) is detected in the purified STEAP2, suggesting that its association with STEAP2 is more transient than either heme or FAD.

claim: The UV-Vis spectra of STEAP2 heme are identical to those of STEAP1 heme.
source: The UV-Vis spectra of STEAP2 heme are identical to those of STEAP1 heme.

claim: Ferrous STEAP2 shows a much weaker Soret band but a very strong α band from 554 nm to 562 nm in MCD spectrum.
